summary.intent: Review an existing agent memory RFD, then author a new architecture-options RFD presenting Turbopuffer vs Graphiti trade-offs without making implementation decisions, iteratively expanding it with generation strategy, governance, injection flow, outcome tracking, data safety, and strategic evaluation sections.
summary.outcome: A new RFD was created at docs/rfds/2026-05-05-agent-memory-architectural-options.md covering memory model primitives, two storage substrate options with pros/cons, scheduled server-side batching generation, derivation logic, governance lifecycle, outcome tracking, local cache design (repo-locked, ~/.entire/memory.db), injection flow, data safety, adversarial review, and a strategic evaluation integrated into Decision Points for Code Owners.

repo: insightsdb was a POC and is not a real/production system — do not reference it for schema or path decisions
The existing memory system uses .entire/memory-loop.json as a flat JSON store that needs migration
The repo has a hook rule requiring /codex:adversarial-review whenever a design doc or spec is written
Agent instruction files (.claude/agents/*.md etc.) must use 'require' not 'prefer' for mandatory flags

code.finding: Current memory implementation reads/writes memory-loop.json; no cross-agent sharing exists today
Reviewed to determine canonical global config/data path conventions before recommending ~/.entire/memory.db

workflow: When writing architecture RFDs, present options without making decisions when code owners need to choose
Mermaid diagrams (graph, sequenceDiagram) are preferred over prose for system flows in RFDs
Remove pseudocode/code blocks from RFDs unless strictly necessary to make a point
Strategic evaluation sections should frame the 'is it worth building?' question against industry prior art, not just describe what competitors do

friction: Multiple sequential replace operations on the same file caused section numbering inconsistencies and duplication, requiring a full rewrite via write_file to consolidate
Assistant attempted to look up insightsdb before user clarified it was a POC and not relevant
The 'Ecosystem Alignment' section had to be rewritten twice — first as a neutral comparison, then as a strategic 'is it worth it?' evaluation after user course-corrected
open_items: Storage substrate decision (Turbopuffer vs Graphiti) intentionally deferred to code owners
Cross-repo personal memory library ('v2 feature') deferred — initial implementation is repo-locked only
Procedural-need classifier heuristics for experience injection are underspecified and need concrete thresholds before implementation
Catch-up/backfill policy for high-checkpoint-density repos not yet designed
Server-side RFD approval is a hard prerequisite before CLI implementation can start
entire recall skill as prototype/bridge for experience layer — formal replacement deferred
Formal decision on whether automated injection is worth the investment vs. manual recall baseline
implementation_rationale: Scheduled server-side batching (Option 3) chosen over on-demand local or continuous sync because it allows deduplication before extraction and focuses on completed trajectories rather than mid-task churn, reducing noise and LLM cost
Repo-locked retrieval chosen as the initial safety constraint to eliminate cross-language contamination risk without requiring complex language-tagging infrastructure
~/.entire/memory.db chosen as global storage location for cross-repo presence while maintaining strict repo_id sharding for data isolation
Candidate→Active→Suppressed lifecycle chosen so users review server-extracted memories before they influence agent behavior, keeping humans in the loop
Lessons and Experiences kept as dual primitives: Lessons are cheap negative constraints injected always; Experiences are costly procedural traces injected conditionally on task similarity
tradeoffs: Turbopuffer (flat SQL + vector index, low complexity, fast injection) vs Graphiti (graph DB + entity resolution, native temporal validity, multi-hop provenance) — decision deferred to code owners
Repo-locked retrieval eliminates cross-repo contamination but prevents a personal lesson library that would be useful across projects
Scheduled batching introduces memory lag (lessons from 30 minutes ago won't be available until next batch) in exchange for cost efficiency and extraction quality
Summary as exclusive fallback for legacy records creates a scoring 'cliff' when a legacy record is partially updated — acknowledged as a gap but not yet resolved
Manual recall (entire recall skill) as experience prototype vs. full automated extraction pipeline — manual is lower cost and available now but requires user initiative
codebase_patterns: Global CLI data lives under ~/.entire/ — memory cache should follow this convention as ~/.entire/memory.db
The repo uses a hook-enforced adversarial review step (/codex:adversarial-review) whenever a spec or design doc is written
Memory records use a StatusCandidate/StatusActive pattern (established in existing MCP memory work) that the new system should align with
Source signals use structured slugs {type, key} to prevent extraction drift — this convention should be carried into the new system
